title: EPA to Repeal Power Plant Emission Rules, Sparking Legal Battle
summary:
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is expected to repeal rules that limit planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas. Administrator Lee Zeldin said the move would remove billions of dollars in costs for the industry and help "unleash" American energy. The announcement could come as soon as Monday, according to two people familiar with the proposal.

The rule change represents a fundamental shift from efforts by Democratic Presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama to address climate change and clean up industrial pollution, often in low-income and majority Black or Hispanic communities. It is also expected to face immediate legal challenges. The people familiar with the proposal spoke on condition of anonymity because the final rule had not yet been made public. The EPA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Zeldin, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Energy Secretary Chris Wright are hosting a G20 ministerial meeting on "energy abundance" in Houston, where the rule change is set to be announced. The site is both a nod to the important role the oil-rich state plays in the energy industry and a potential snub of European and other international allies in attendance who have pursued environmentally friendly policies that the Trump administration has moved to undo.

Republican President Donald Trump called climate change "the greatest con job ever perpetrated on the world" at a speech to the United Nations last year, and his administration withdrew the U.S. — for the second time — from the 2015 Paris climate accord that sets voluntary goals to curb planet-warming emissions. Trump has boasted of U.S. energy abundance even as the Iran war continues to disrupt global fuel markets and gas prices top $4.31 a gallon, up more than a dollar from a year ago.

The rollbacks are meant to fulfill Trump's repeated pledge to "unleash American energy" and make it easier for utilities to supply electricity for homes and businesses. The power plant rule is among nearly three dozen environmental regulations that Zeldin targeted in early 2025 when he announced what he called the "most consequential day of deregulation in American history." Zeldin said in proposing the new rules last year that they were meant to end the Biden and Obama administrations' "war on so much of our U.S. domestic energy supply."

Environmental and public health groups called the rollbacks dangerous and vowed to challenge the rules in court. "Tearing down our national protections against climate pollution from power plants will have enormous costs for the health, safety and well-being of families across the country," said Vickie Patton, general counsel for the Environmental Defense Fund. "Americans everywhere are already suffering from record-breaking heat, more dangerous floods and storms, and skyrocketing insurance costs." Patton said the EPA has a legal responsibility to protect the public from harmful pollution, adding that "clean, affordable and reliable technologies are widely available to power our homes and businesses."

Coal, gas and oil-fired power plants are responsible for about one-quarter of the nation's total climate pollution, second only to the transportation sector. The rules targeted by Trump's EPA could prevent an estimated 30,000 deaths and save $275 billion each year they are in effect, according to an Associated Press examination last year. Even a partial dismantling of the rules would mean more pollutants such as smog, mercury and lead — and especially more tiny airborne particles that can lodge in lungs and cause health problems. It would also mean higher emissions of greenhouse gases, driving Earth's warming to deadlier levels.

Biden had made fighting climate change a hallmark of his presidency. Coal-fired power plants would have been forced to capture smokestack emissions or shut down under a strict EPA rule issued in 2024. Those rules are now being upended. In its proposal last year, the Trump EPA argued that carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases from fossil fuel-fired power plants "do not contribute significantly to dangerous pollution" or climate change and therefore do not meet a threshold under the Clean Air Act for regulatory action. Greenhouse gas emissions from coal and gas-fired plants "are a small and decreasing part of global emissions," the EPA said. Zeldin said the Biden-era rules were designed to "suffocate our economy in order to protect the environment," with the intent to regulate the coal industry "out of existence" and make it "disappear."
why_it_matters: Electricity runs homes and schools, and the pollution from making it affects the air everyone breathes — so this fight will decide how much the U.S. government is allowed to do about climate change and public health in the coming years.

background_read: The EPA (the Environmental Protection Agency, the U.S. government agency created in 1970 to write and enforce pollution rules) was established under President Richard Nixon after disasters such as the Cuyahoga River catching fire pushed Congress to act.

The Clean Air Act (the main U.S. air pollution law, passed in 1970 and updated in 1990) has been used for decades to phase out leaded gasoline and to force power plants to cut pollutants such as mercury and smog-forming chemicals.

In 2022 the Supreme Court ruled in West Virginia v. EPA that the agency could not use the Clean Air Act to force a nationwide shift away from coal-fired electricity, which is one reason later rules were written to target individual plants instead.

The Paris climate accord (a 2015 agreement in which nearly 200 countries set voluntary goals to slow global warming) has been joined and left by the U.S. depending on who is president — Trump pulled out during his first term, Biden rejoined, and Trump withdrew again.

Rules on power plant pollution have see-sawed for decades: each administration writes new ones, industry and environmental groups sue, and the courts end up deciding how far the EPA's authority actually reaches.

perspectives.description: Zeldin and utility companies argue the old rules cost billions, push up electricity prices and threaten reliable power. They say the Clean Air Act was never meant to regulate carbon dioxide from power plants, and that American energy should be 'unleashed' rather than restricted.

Groups like the Environmental Defense Fund say repealing the rules means more smog, mercury, lead and fine particles that lodge in lungs, especially hurting families near plants. They point to record heat, worse floods and rising insurance costs, and argue clean technology is already available.

U.S. air and climate policy has always swung with the party in the White House, and the courts often end up deciding the limits of the EPA's power. The 2022 Supreme Court ruling already narrowed how the Clean Air Act can be used, so this repeal fits a longer pattern of regulation and rollback rather than being a one-off event.

The rule will almost certainly be challenged in court, and the outcome could stand for years, shaping what future administrations can do. Meanwhile the U.S. has stepped back from the Paris accord again, raising the question of whether states, cities or private companies will cut emissions on their own.
